lead: A DFA recognises a language by moving between states. A regular expression describes the same language as a pattern. Converting one to the other lets you prove equality, feed a pattern to a tool, or simplify a machine. The method is to write one equation per state, then solve the equations with Arden's theorem. A graphical shortcut, state elimination, does the same job by deleting states one at a time. Compilers and text tools use this link when they turn token patterns into matching code.
prereq: You need: DFA and transition diagrams from Unit 1, and the operators of regular expressions from Chapter 2.1.

blocks.text: For a DFA M = (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F), write one equation for each state q. The variable q stands for the language of all strings that take M from q to a final state. Every outgoing transition q --a→ p adds the term a·p: symbol a followed by any string that works from p. If q is final, also add ε, because the empty string is already at a final state. The equation is:
q = Σ<sub>a ∈ Σ, δ(q,a)=p</sub> a·p + (ε if q ∈ F)
blocks.where: q and p are states used as language variables; a·p is concatenation of the one-symbol string a with the language p; + is union; ε is the empty string; δ is the transition function.

items: List every state and give each one a variable.
For each state, collect one term per outgoing edge. Combine edges with the same destination as (a+b)p.
Add ε only in the equation of a final state.
Solve the equations for the start state q0. The expression you get is the required regular expression.

blocks.text: This method is mechanical: a two-state DFA gives two equations; a three-state DFA gives three equations. Use it when the automaton is small. For a large drawing, state elimination is faster.
Arden's theorem solves one equation with one unknown language. Suppose X is unknown, P and Q are known languages, and ε ∉ P. Then:
X = Q + P X  ⇒  X = P* Q,    X = Q + X P  ⇒  X = Q P*
blocks.where: X, P, Q are languages; P* is zero or more repetitions of P; the rule needs ε ∉ P.

blocks.text: In X = Q + P X, strings either stop via Q or do one P then solve X again. Repeated substitution gives X = Q + P Q + P P Q + … = (ε + P + P P + …) Q = P* Q. The condition ε ∉ P says P cannot produce the empty string, so every trip around the loop consumes at least one input symbol. If P can be ε, the repeated substitution never makes progress and the simple solution may fail. The right-side form is solved by Q P*: here the loop is written after X. Identify the form before applying the formula. Some syllabi call it Arden's lemma.

State elimination is the same algebra drawn on the transition graph. It removes one state at a time. Add a new start state with an ε-edge to the old start, and a new final state with ε-edges from every old final state. Then delete each old state q. For every state i with an edge into q and every state j with an edge out of q, create or extend the edge i→j by the expression:

blocks.where: R<sub>ab</sub> is the label on the edge from a to b, or ∅ if there is no edge; R<sub>qq</sub> is the label of q's self-loop, or ∅ if there is none; ∅* = ε, so a state with no self-loop just contributes R<sub>iq</sub> R<sub>qj</sub>; * allows the loop to repeat any number of times.

items: Pick a state q to remove, never the new start or new final.
For each predecessor i and successor j of q, add the path i→q→j. The label is R<sub>ij</sub> + R<sub>iq</sub> (R<sub>qq</sub>)* R<sub>qj</sub>.
Delete q and all its edges.
Repeat until only the new start and new final remain. Read the single remaining label as the regular expression.

blocks.text: Order can change the intermediate expression but not the language. Keep the graph small to avoid long labels.

figure.caption: The DFA for binary strings ending in 1: q0 is the start state and q1 is final. The self-loops keep the current last bit; the edge q0→q1 records a 1.

spec.aria: A two-state DFA for binary strings ending in 1: q0 is start and q1 is final, with self-loops labelled 0 and 1.

examples.question: Convert the DFA M over Σ={0,1} with states q0 (start) and q1 (final), and transitions q0--0→q0, q0--1→q1, q1--0→q0, q1--1→q1, into a regular expression using state equations and Arden's theorem.
steps: Write one equation per state. For q0: q0 = 0 q0 + 1 q1. For q1: q1 = 0 q0 + 1 q1 + ε.
Solve q0 in terms of q1. Rewrite q0 = 1 q1 + 0 q0. This is X = Q + P X with X=q0, Q=1 q1, P=0. Since ε ∉ {0}, Arden gives q0 = 0* 1 q1.
Substitute q0 into the q1 equation: q1 = ε + 0(0* 1 q1) + 1 q1.
Apply Arden with X=q1, Q=ε, P=0*1. Every string in 0*1 ends in 1, so ε ∉ P. Thus q1 = (0*1)* ε = (0*1)*.
Use the identity (0*1)* 0*1 = (0+1)*1, from the identities chapter.
examples.answer: The regular expression is (0+1)*1, the set of binary strings ending in 1.

traps: In X = Q + P X, the star goes on P: X = P* Q, not Q* P. The other side X = Q + X P gives X = Q P*.
Add ε only to the equation of a final state, not to every equation.
Do not drop self-loops: a self-loop q --a→ q contributes a q.
Arden's rule needs ε ∉ P. If P contains ε, the simple star formula is not justified.
In state elimination, the new edge label order is R<sub>iq</sub> (R<sub>qq</sub>)* R<sub>qj</sub>; reversing it changes the language.

quiz.q: State Arden's theorem for the equation X = Q + P X.
quiz.a: If ε ∉ P, then X = Q + P X has the unique solution X = P* Q.

quiz.q: Why does Arden's theorem require ε ∉ P?
quiz.a: If ε ∈ P, the loop can repeat without consuming input, so repeated substitution does not force a unique solution. The simple formula P*Q may fail.

quiz.q: For q0 = (0+1)q0 + ε with q0 final, find q0.
In the worked example, after q0=0*1q1, what equation for q1 remains after substitution?
A one-state DFA has start state q0, final state q0, transitions 0 and 1 back to q0. Write its equation and solve.
A student writes q1 = ε + 0q0 + 1q1 and applies X = Q + X P with P=1. What is wrong?
quiz.a: The loop term is 1q1, which is P X, not X P. Use X = Q + P X with P=1, Q=ε+0q0; q1 = 1*(ε+0q0).

quiz.q: In state elimination, why is R<sub>qq</sub> starred in R<sub>ij</sub> + R<sub>iq</sub> (R<sub>qq</sub>)* R<sub>qj</sub>?
quiz.a: R<sub>qq</sub> is the loop on q; the path may go around it zero or more times before leaving along R<sub>qj</sub>. The star records that repetition.

quiz.q: Where is ε added in the state equations?
quiz.a: Only in the equation of a final state, because the empty string is accepted at that state.

beyond: Not for the exam. Tools such as lex and re2c convert regular expressions to DFAs, then minimise them, because a DFA runs in time proportional to the input with no backtracking. Modern regex engines often use backtracking for features beyond regular languages, which is why a pattern can be fast on one input and slow on another. State elimination also appears in model checking, where a finite-state system is turned into an algebraic description. Search for 'Brzozowski derivatives' to see another way to convert automata to expressions, and 'Thompson construction' for the reverse direction.
